name: Guess the Number
desc: A real game: scripted guesses, warmer-or-colder verdicts, an attempt counter.

steps.title: The game plan
steps.text:
You're building a real guessing game. The computer holds a secret number. Three guesses walk in, one by one, and the game judges each: too low, too high, or correct — counting attempts along the way.

The whole game is below. You don't need to memorize it. Just notice the shape: setup at the top, a loop in the middle, a three-way judge inside. You'll build every piece yourself in the next steps.
steps.hint: No action needed — just read. The tour below names every part you will build.

steps.title: Welcome the player
steps.text: Every game greets its player. The starter below runs fine, but its welcome is a sad little "...". Change that placeholder into the real greeting from the goal box. Then press Run.
steps.hint: Change only the text between the quotes: fmt.Println("Guess my number (1-10)!") — mind the exclamation mark.

steps.title: The judge is silent
steps.text: Someone built the game but forgot the happy ending: guesses get judged too low or too high, and then... nothing. A correct guess prints silence. The goal shows what SHOULD happen. Add the missing branch so a correct guess celebrates.
steps.hint: After the else-if block closes, add: } else { then the Correct Println, then }. The attempts variable is already counting for you.

3 is too low
9 is too high
Correct in 3 tries!

steps.title: Lay the foundation
steps.text: Before any judging, the game needs its foundation: greet the player, load the list of guesses, peek at the first one. Six lines, all shuffled. A real program this time — the correct order compiles and runs.
steps.hint: package first, import second, func main opens the door, the greeting prints first, the list loads before anything peeks at it, and the lone brace closes main last.

steps.title: Deliver the verdict
steps.text: The setup stands. Now the judge: a three-way verdict for each guess — too low, too high, or correct. Pick the real lines from the pool (two impostors are mixed in) and place them in order.
steps.hint: if opens, else-if continues, else closes the debate. The final lone brace closes the if — and watch out for the line that forgot to print the guess.

steps.title: Spot the cheat
steps.text: Playtesters keep winning on the first try. Suspicious. Somewhere in this game there's a line that leaks the secret to the player before they guess. Tap it.
steps.hint: The leak is a Println that mentions the secret. Honest games never print it.

steps.title: Opening night
steps.text: The whole game, assembled — secret, guesses, counter, loop, judge. Nothing missing, nothing broken. Press Run and watch your game play all three rounds.
steps.hint: No edits needed. Just press Run and enjoy the show.

steps.text: The game runs and celebrates — but it lies about the score: it claims 2 tries when all three guesses played. The counter line is in the wrong place: it ticks AFTER the verdict instead of BEFORE it. Move one line so the count is honest.
steps.hint: attempts++ sits at the bottom of the loop, after the judge. Move it to the top of the loop, before the if. Same line, different home.

name: Word Counter
desc: A real tally: split a sentence, count every word, crown the winner.

steps.title: The plan
steps.text: You're building a word counter: split a sentence, tally every word in a map, scan for the champion. The whole program is below — setup, tally loop, winner scan. You'll build every piece yourself next.
steps.hint: No action needed — just read. Fields splits, the map tallies, the scan crowns.

steps.title: How many words?
steps.text: First question, simplest tool: strings.Fields splits on ANY whitespace — spaces, tabs, newlines, doubles. Our sentence holds 8 words. Predict, then run. No edits — just feel Fields.
steps.hint: Count them on your fingers: go-is-fun-go-is-fast-go-rules. Eight.

steps.title: Split on air
steps.text: Someone split on commas — but the sentence has no commas, so the whole thing lands in ONE chunk and the count reads 1. The goal is 8. Swap the comma-split for Fields, then run.
steps.hint: strings.Split(s, ",") sees zero commas and returns one giant chunk. Fields sees whitespace.

steps.title: Tally loop
steps.text: The engine room: split, walk, bump. Assemble the full mini-program — it prints the whole tally map (Go prints maps sorted by key, so the output is stable).
steps.hint: Imports ride together in one block. The map is born empty, the loop bumps, the print shows all.

steps.title: Crown the winner
steps.text: The tally stands. Now scan for the champion: strictly-greater keeps the FIRST max it meets. Pick the true lines — one impostor crowns ties wrongly, another assigns backwards.
steps.hint: Strictly greater (>) keeps the first champion. >= would crown the LAST tied word instead.

steps.title: The nil tally
steps.text: The counter panics before counting a single word. The map was declared but never made — reading a nil map is fine, writing to it explodes. Tap the line writing to thin air.
steps.hint: var counts map[string]int is a signpost with no wall. Which line hangs a coat on it?
steps.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var counts map[string]int
	counts["go"]++
	fmt.Println(counts["go"])
}

steps.title: Opening night
steps.text: The whole counter, assembled — split, tally, crown. 'go' appears 3 times, nothing else tops 2. Predict the champion pair, then run.
steps.hint: go-go-go: three sightings. Strictly-greater keeps the first max — and nothing ties it.

name: Todo CLI
desc: A real task list: structs, slices, and the range-copy trap.

steps.title: The plan
steps.text: You're building a todo list: a Task struct (title + done flag), a slice holding two tasks, one marked finished, and a filter printing what's left. Full program below — structs, append,(indexing, and a range filter you'll assemble yourself.
steps.hint: No action needed — just read. Struct shapes the data, the slice holds it, the loop filters it.

steps.title: Add two
steps.text: Two tasks appended, zero finished. Predict the count line, then run. Notice the append style: two struct literals in ONE call.
steps.hint: Two appends, one call, no finishing yet. The count is honest.

steps.title: Done means done
steps.text: The loop 'finishes' every task — yet both print false. range hands you COPIES: t.Done = true decorates a copy and throws it away. The goal is true true. Rewrite the loop to write through indexes, then run.
steps.hint: for i := range tasks, then tasks[i].Done = true. Index in, write through — copies can't save you.

steps.title: List the pending
steps.text: Filter and print: walk both tasks, keep the unfinished titles, join them. Assemble the full program — it prints exactly one line: the survivor.
steps.hint: Type rides up top, imports in a block, the filter keeps only !Done, Join glues the survivors.

steps.title: Finish one
steps.text: Mark 'ship it' done by TITLE: walk with indexes, compare, write through. Pick the true lines — one impostor ranges copies again, another writes the copy.
steps.hint: Range copies won't save you twice — index in with i, compare tasks[i].Title, write tasks[i].Done.

steps.title: The phantom index
steps.text: Two tasks in the list — and one line reaches for a third. Slot 2 does not exist, and Go answers with a panic instead of garbage. Tap the line grabbing the ghost.
steps.hint: Two tenants, slots 0 and 1. Which line knocks on slot 2?

steps.title: Opening night
steps.text: The whole list, assembled — two tasks in, first one finished, filter the rest. Predict the final line, then run.
steps.hint: tasks[0] is done, tasks[1] survives the filter. One left, by name.

name: JSON Rescue
desc: A real decoder: structs, tags, and the errors you must not swallow.

steps.title: The plan
steps.text: You're decoding real JSON: a blob describing a repo, a struct with tags telling each field where to land, an error check guarding the door, and a print of the result. Full program below — tags do the mapping, err does the guarding.
steps.hint: No action needed — just read. Tags map, Unmarshal fills, err guards, print shows.

steps.title: Read the label
steps.text: Decode and print just the title. The tag matches, the JSON is valid, the door is guarded. Predict the word, then run.
steps.hint: title tag meets title key. One word comes out.

steps.title: Deaf tags
steps.text: The stars arrive, the title doesn't: it prints ' has 6 stars' — a ghost with a count. The Title tag listens on 'name' while the JSON shouts 'title'. Tags are exact-match contracts. Fix the one wrong word, then run.
steps.hint: json:"name" hears nothing because the blob says title. Retune the tag to title.

steps.title: Guard the door
steps.text: Decode into a plain map and guard the door: bad JSON must print 'bad json', good JSON prints the value. Assemble the full program — error check included, no swallowing.
steps.hint: Unmarshal first, interrogate err second, use the map third. The guard returns early.

steps.title: Unmarshal into what?
steps.text: json.Unmarshal needs a HOME for the data — and here is a proper gotcha: decoding a JSON object into a NIL map. Assignment to a nil map panics, but what does Unmarshal do?
steps.hint: Unmarshal OWNS the map it fills. Who makes it — you, or the decoder?

options: It allocates and fills — no panic
quiz.why: Unmarshal owns the map it fills: nil map plus a JSON object comes back freshly made. Assignment panics, unmarshaling provides — opposite rules, same nil.

steps.title: The silent failure
steps.text: Broken JSON in, zero values out — and NOT A WORD about it. The Unmarshal call's error return floats into the void, unchecked. Tap the line that swallows the failure.
steps.hint: Somebody called a function that returns an error and looked away. Which line?

steps.title: Opening night
steps.text: The whole rescue, assembled — tags tuned, door guarded, result printed. Predict the final line, then run.
steps.hint: title tag meets title key, stars land as 6. One clean line out.

name: Task CLI
desc: A real command line: usage guards, switch dispatch, numbered lists.

steps.title: The plan
steps.text: You're building a real command line: os.Args carries the words, a usage guard catches empty hands, a switch dispatches commands, unknown words get a verdict. Full program below — playground passes NO arguments, so keep that in mind for the next step.
steps.hint: No action needed — just read. [0] is the program's own path; real words start at [1].

steps.title: First run
steps.text: Playground passes NO arguments: os.Args holds only the exe path, args is empty, and the usage guard fires before the switch. Predict the handshake line, then run. No edits.
steps.hint: No args in the playground: the len guard fires first. The handshake, exactly as written.

steps.title: Dispatch table
steps.text: The judge of the CLI: a switch on the command. Assemble the list branch as a full program — it prints every task numbered from 1.
steps.hint: Switch opens on cmd, the list branch numbers from i+1, default catches strangers, braces close switch then main.

steps.title: Off by one
steps.text: The list prints '0 write tests' — machines count from 0, humans queue from 1. Numbered lists start at i+1. Predict the human numbering, then fix one expression.
steps.hint: Machines count from 0, humans from 1: numbered lists print i+1.

steps.title: Add branch
steps.text: New command: add takes a task — but ONLY with a word present. Bare 'add' must print 'add what?' and stop. Pick the true lines; one impostor guards the wrong bound, another echoes the command instead of the task.
steps.hint: args[0] is the command itself — the task lives at [1], which exists only when len is 2+.

steps.title: Wrong slot
steps.text: Every run prints 'unknown command: /tmp/go-build...' — it dispatches on its OWN path. os.Args[0] is the exe; real words start at [1]. Tap the line reading the wrong slot.
steps.hint: args[0] is the program's own path. Which line crowns it commander?

steps.title: Why len check first?
steps.text: args[1] with no arguments handed over: what does Go do?
steps.hint: Slices don't negotiate. What happens at index 1 of length 1?

quiz.why: os.Args is just a slice, and [1] on a 1-long slice panics. Guard len BEFORE indexing — usage-first is the CLI author's handshake.

steps.title: Opening night
steps.text: The whole CLI, assembled — usage guard, switch, add branch, list branch, stranger default. Playground hands it nothing, so opening night prints the handshake. Predict it, then run.
steps.hint: No args, so the guard fires first. The handshake, exactly as written.

name: Mini Markdown
desc: A real renderer: prefixes in, HTML out, one pass.

steps.title: The plan
steps.text: A tiny renderer: split markdown into lines, match each prefix, emit HTML into a strings.Builder. Three rules (# goes h1, - goes li, everything else goes p), one pass, no dependencies. Full program below.
steps.hint: No action needed — just read. Split, match, emit. The switch reads prefixes; Builder collects.

steps.title: First tag
steps.text: One line in, one tag out: render('# Hi') prints a single h1. Predict the exact bytes (tags included), then run.
steps.hint: TrimPrefix eats '# ', the format wraps the rest. Exact bytes.

steps.title: Greedy prefix
steps.text: '## Sub' is NOT our h1 (we only crown '# ' with the space) — but the starter matches bare '#' and crowns it anyway. One space is the whole bug. Predict the TRUE rendering, then fix the prefix.
steps.hint: '#' matches '##' too — demand the space.

steps.title: Assemble the switch
steps.text: The whole matcher, shuffled: main calls, render matches — h1 branch, li branch, default paragraph. Assemble all twenty lines.
steps.hint: main calls first (legal Go), render matches after: h1 branch, li branch, default paragraph, close everything in order.

steps.title: List items
steps.text: The li branch, exact: match '- ' prefix, trim it, emit the tag WITH its newline — a missing newline glues items into one blob. Pick the true lines; one impostor drops the newline, another trims the wrong end.
steps.hint: TrimPrefix eats the marker; the newline ends the line. TrimSuffix eats the wrong end; missing newline glues the list.

steps.title: The glued list
steps.text:
Two items in, ONE blob out: '
  • a
  • b
    • ' on a single line. The li Fprintf lost its newline — every item glues to the last. Tap the line missing its newline.
steps.hint: One Fprintf ends without a newline. Which tag's line never breaks?

steps.title: Why Builder?
steps.text: Why strings.Builder instead of s += tag, over and over?
steps.hint: Immutable means every += rebuilds the world. Who avoids that?

options: += copies the whole prefix every time (O(n²))
quiz.why: Strings are immutable: s += x copies everything so far, every time — quadratic. Builder buffers and materializes once: O(n). Same letters, honest cost.

steps.title: Opening night
steps.text: The whole renderer, assembled — split, match all three, emit, print. Predict the four lines exactly, then run.
steps.hint: h1, li, li, p — in order, each terminated.
